Case holds a statutory tenant's widow may continue possession under the Emergency Rent Laws after his death; lodger/boarder treatment is dicta quoted from May v. Dermont, not this case's holding, so it does not itself decide the character of a letting.

holding_summary: Defendant, who as a landlord had sublet a furnished apartment to a third party for profit and was not himself in occupation, was not a statutory tenant entitled to Emergency Rent Law protection; because he permitted his subtenant to hold over and plaintiff elected to hold him liable, he was a holdover tenant as a matter of law and owed rent for the two months after his lease expired.

This defendant had neither possession nor right to possession so long as his subtenant continued to live in the apartment and paid rent.

holding_summary: Plaintiff, who held two rooms and a bath in a residence under a written lease at monthly rent paid in advance, was wrongfully evicted by the landlord's self-help acts (cutting off heat and light) before the paid-up period expired; the court held he could sue in trespass rather than solely on the covenant for quiet enjoyment, that a finding of wrongful eviction supports at least nominal damages, and reversed the compulsory nonsuit.

quotes.text: At the trial it appeared that the plaintiff occupied two rooms and a bath in a residence in the city of Philadelphia. He was in possession under a written lease at rental of 116.00 per month payable in advance.
One who wrongfully invades the rights of another is a trespasser, and this rule applies to the unlawful invasion of the rights of a tenant by his landlord.
If the jury should determine that the tenant had been wrongfully evicted, nominal damages at least would follow, even if no other elements of damage had been proved.
